phonemes.desc: Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ] with a dot below in Yoruba orthography; the dot below marks the phoneme /ʃ/, distinct from /s/.
Open central vowel [a] with low tone.
Velar nasal [ŋ] followed by voiced velar stop [g] and close back rounded vowel [o] with high tone; the syllable is nasalised.

pronunciation.approximation: SHAH-ngoh — low 'sha', then a sharp high 'ngoh' with the final syllable slightly nasal.

kin.label: Yoruba
kin.form: Ṣàngó, the deified fourth king of Oyo and orixá of thunder and fire.

kin.label: Brazilian Candomblé
kin.form: Xangô, the just king who wields the double-headed axe and judges disputes.

kin.label: Cuban Santería
kin.form: Changó, the dancer, drummer, and lord of lightning.

pronunciation.note: Ṣàngó is Tier 1: the dot below ṣ and the acute accent on ó are distinctive features the ASCII form loses, the acute preserving the high tone of the final syllable. The dot below ṣ marks the historical/orthographic distinction of the Yoruba 's' series.

domains.title: Thunder and Justice
domains.subtitle: Fire, Royalty, and the Drum
domains.lead: Ṣàngó is the thunder-god and the deified fourth king of the Ọ̀yọ́ Empire — the fire that strikes from heaven and the drumbeat that brings the possessed to their feet. His justice is public and swift: the oath-breaker, the thief, and the liar hear him before they see him. In life a warrior-king, in death he became the storm itself.

cards.name: Lightning
cards.desc: He strikes the liar, the thief, and the oath-breaker; his fire is both weapon and verdict.

cards.name: Double-Headed Axe
cards.desc: The ọ̀ṣẹ́ Ṣàngó — the double-axe dance wand, his emblem of royal justice and the power to split heaven and earth.

cards.name: Royal Charisma
cards.desc: He was king before he was god; his worship links divine power to political authority.

cards.name: Drum and Dance
cards.desc: The bàtá drum calls him down; possession by Ṣàngó begins in the shoulders and feet.

symbols.name: Thunderstones (ẹ̀dùn àrá)
symbols.meaning: 'Thunder stones' — prehistoric stone axes kept in his shrines as the thunderbolts he hurled to earth; collecting one is collecting his signature.

symbols.name: Double-headed axe (ọ̀ṣẹ́ Ṣàngó)
symbols.meaning: The emblem of his kingship and his power to render judgment; carved dance wands of it are carried by the possessed.

symbols.name: Bàtá drum
symbols.meaning: The hourglass drum whose pitch bends under the arm — the drum language that summons him and encodes the history of Ọ̀yọ́.

symbols.name: Red and white beads
symbols.meaning: The colours of fire, blood, and royal authority; his initiates wear them in double strands.

mythology.lead: Ṣàngó's mythology moves between the palace and the sky. He is a king who could not govern his own household, a husband of powerful and dangerous wives, and a storm whose justice is as dramatic as its noise.

myths.title: The Fourth Aláàfin of Ọ̀yọ́
myths.text: Ṣàngó was the fourth Aláàfin — king — of Ọ̀yọ́, and the traditions collected by Samuel Johnson (The History of the Yorubas, 1921), checked against the chronicles analysed by Robin Law (The Oyo Empire, 1977), make him a historical ruler later wrapped in divinity. His capital was at Koso, and his cult grew from the worship of a deified king: subsequent Aláàfins ruled as his heirs, and the Ṣàngó festival at Ọ̀yọ́ remains an act of state as much as of religion. The sources disagree about his end — some say he hanged himself in defeat, others that his own fire consumed him and he ascended bodily — and the people of Koso answered the shameful version with a proud folk etymology: Koso, they said, means 'he did not hang'. Whatever happened in history, mythology turned a failed king into an eternal verdict from the sky.

myths.title: The Fire That Consumed the Palace
myths.text: Johnson's chronicle credits Ṣàngó with a fearful sorcery: charms that breathed fire on his enemies. In the most told episode, his own overreaching turned the weapon inward — the fire that burned his foes spread through his palace and his household, and the king who had terrorised Ọ̀yọ́ with thunder-magic died, or fled, by the same element (Johnson 1921; Law 1977 treats the traditions with scholarly reserve). Later Ifá verses and praise-chants amplify the tale into cosmic register: Ṣàngó did not merely wield fire, he was fire, and he left the earth by immolating himself into the storm. The palace fires of the chronicle became, in worship, the lightning of the sky. The legend reads like a parable of charisma — the force that makes a king irresistible is the force that finally consumes him, and only deification survives the burning.

myths.title: Three Wives of Thunder
myths.text: Ṣàngó's household is a small pantheon, and its myths are the corpus's sharpest studies of desire and power. Ọbà, his first wife, tried to win back his wandering love by cutting off her ear to season his stew — the myth's warning is against sacrificing identity for affection. Ọṣun won him with honey, brass, and laughter, becoming the one being who can calm his rage. Ọya, his favourite in war, learned the secret of fire and lightning from him and did not abandon him in disgrace. His children by them inherit his fire; his cult inherits their lessons. The stories, told across Ifá verses, praise-songs, and diaspora liturgies (Verger 1981; Mason), make the thunderer's marriage bed the site where three kinds of female power — devotion, sweetness, and fury — each take the measure of male force and outlast it.

myths.title: The Thunder That Hears Oaths
myths.text: In Yoruba courts and shrines, oaths sworn in Ṣàngó's name were binding because the thunder-god was believed to strike perjurers — and the fear was not merely supernatural. Law notes that royal authority in Ọ̀yọ́ leaned on the cult: the king who could call the storm to witness promises made his own word unbreakable, and his priests kept the thunderstones (prehistoric celts) that proved the strikes were real (Law 1977; Bascom 1969). Even today, devotees say that a liar who swears falsely by Ṣàngó will be found out by fire. Even where courts have replaced oaths, devotees still decline to swear falsely by his name, and lightning still makes honest witnesses of the frightened. His justice is swift, public, and terrifying — the sky itself made a witness to human promises, and a penalty no wall could delay.

myths.title: The Drum That Calls the King Down
myths.text: Priestly tradition holds that the bàtá drum was Ṣàngó's before it was anyone's: the hourglass drum whose pitch bends under the player's arm speaks a language the thunder-king cannot refuse, and at his festivals the drummers 'talk' him down into the dancers (Mason, Four New World Yoruba Rituals; Drewal 1992). Possession by Ṣàngó begins in the shoulders and feet — the stamping, whirling dance of a warrior — and the possessed speak with his voice, rendering judgment and greeting the crowd as a king greets subjects. The mythology completes itself here: the king who died left no tomb to visit, so his people built a throne of rhythm. The drummers themselves are minor royalty of the cult, addressed with titles and fed before the crowd. When the bàtá plays, Ọ̀yọ́ has a king again, and the storm walks in human form.

lore.syncretism: In Cuban Santería, Ṣàngó became Changó, one of the most beloved orishas, merged with Santa Bárbara because of her lightning, her tower, and her protection of the faithful — his feast, 4 December, is hers as well. In Brazilian Candomblé he is Xangô, syncretised in the Ketu nation with São Jerônimo, the thunder-voiced doctor of the Church. The diaspora preserved and amplified what Ọ̀yọ́ began: the union of kingship, rhythm, and storm. Where the old empire fell to the Fulani wars of the nineteenth century, its thunder-god reigned on in Havana, Salvador, and Brooklyn — a royal cult that lost its palace and gained an ocean.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ṣàngó is one of the most recognisable orishas in the African diaspora. His image strides through Caribbean and Latin American art, music, and festival; his bàtá drumming — carried by Cuban santeros to stages worldwide — has fed into jazz, salsa, and contemporary percussion. In Nigeria the Ṣàngó Festival in Ọ̀yọ́ draws thousands each year, and the Aláàfin still keeps ritual ties to the deified founder of his line. Politically, Ṣàngó remains a badge of Yoruba royal authority and cultural pride; spiritually, he embodies the demand that justice be as visible and unavoidable as a thunderclap. His double-headed axe has become an emblem of Afro-Atlantic religion itself, recognisable from Lagos to Havana.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ṣàngó is the god who refuses to be ignored. His thunder does not negotiate; it announces. In a world of deferred justice and hidden corruption, he represents the fantasy — and the danger — of immediate consequence. To call on him is to ask that the truth be made loud.

Yet his mythology is also a caution. He was a king who lost control, a husband whose charisma burned the women around him, a storm that could not be aimed with precision. His double-headed axe cuts both ways; the same fire that punishes the liar consumes the proud. Ṣàngó's deepest teaching may be that justice without patience becomes spectacle — and that the thunderclap, however satisfying, is only the beginning of the rain.

lore.archaeology: The Ṣàngó cult centre at Koso, near Ọ̀yọ́ in present-day Nigeria, preserves the ritual memory of the deified king, and the Ṣàngó festival re-enacts his kingship annually. Prehistoric stone celts — the thunderstones his priests collected as his spent bolts — are held in shrines and museum collections; so are brass double-headed axes, bàtá drums, and the red-and-white bead regalia of his initiates. Diaspora terreiros and ilés conserve his dance wands and thunderstone altars, making Ṣàngó one of the best-documented royal cults in African religious history.
